prize_parts.citation: For incorporating firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory, transforming the analysis of the gains from trade and of firm-level trade data.

statement.case_for: Firm heterogeneity and selection changed how trade is modelled and measured. Gains from trade now run through reallocation across firms and exporter selection, and the field has shifted to firm-level microdata. The central contribution is easy to identify: Melitz (2003) is the originating model, and Helpman, Melitz and Yeaple extended it to exporting versus FDI. That makes a two-name award cleaner than most competing ballots. After more than twenty years, the framework's predictions have been confronted with firm-level data from many countries and used widely in policy evaluation. As someone who cares about replicability, I weigh this kind of repeated testing heavily. Having heard colleagues, I now put B026 ahead of my opening first choice, B001. The law-and-finance cross-country regressions face robustness and measurement concerns (revised indices, contested causal readings) that the firm-level trade evidence faces less.
statement.case_against: Credit may extend beyond the credited names. Bernard and Jensen on empirical firm facts, and Eaton and Kortum on quantitative trade, made parallel contributions that this ballot does not credit. Some predictions depend on functional-form assumptions, such as the productivity distribution, and the size of the welfare gains is debated. The field also overlaps with the 2008 trade prize, so the Committee could see this as an extension of recognised ground. If the Committee wants the broadest policy footprint, the monetary framework in B012 has a stronger claim.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B026 first. She sees Melitz (2003) as the central contribution and Helpman as the natural second laureate through his work with Melitz and Yeaple. She treats Redding's quantitative extensions as more derivative, so she leaves him out. She also flags possible overlap with the 2008 trade prize.
responses.response: I agree on the two-name structure, and it is why I now prefer B026. Excluding Redding is defensible if the discovery is the heterogeneous-firm framework itself rather than the later quantitative-spatial work. I would add one caution. The 'derivative' judgment is itself an attribution call, and the Committee should be explicit about it. On the 2008 overlap, I read the 2008 prize as covering scale economies and location. Selection and reallocation across firms is a distinct empirical and theoretical advance, but I do not treat 'trade is due' as merit.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B012 first. He sees Calvo, Taylor and Woodford as the clearest originators of the pricing, contracting and policy-framework elements. He regards the work as mature and of very large policy impact, while admitting that a three-person cut omits Gali, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Gertler and Smets. He also notes that the Taylor rule is closer to a rule of thumb than a deep theoretical result.
responses.response: I accept the scale of influence, and I keep B012 as my first alternative. Two things hold me back from putting it first. Eight credited names and several distinct strands (Calvo pricing, Taylor contracts and the rule, Woodford's synthesis, DSGE estimation) mean any trio will look arbitrary to part of the field. And the framework's empirical performance in the post-2021 inflation episode is still being digested. I agree the Taylor rule's weight is the weakest link in the trio, and that strengthens the case for treating Calvo and Woodford as the core if the Committee goes this way.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B007 first. He argues that collateral constraints and credit amplification are central to how macroeconomists understand cycles and crises. He adds Gertler to Kiyotaki and Moore for the financial-accelerator and intermediary-frictions strand, and notes the overlap with the 2022 prize.
responses.response: Kiyotaki-Moore is a clean, original mechanism, and I do not dispute its influence on post-2008 modelling. My reservation is that the theoretical mechanism is better established than its empirical identification. Several colleagues, including Strömberg, say the same. The 2022 prize also covers neighbouring ground, and adding Gertler brings in the accelerator lineage tied to an existing laureate. I see this as a strong candidate but not clearly stronger than B026, whose predictions have been tested repeatedly against firm-level data. I would want the Committee to say whether the discovery is the collateral mechanism alone or the wider financial-accelerator framework.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee would credit Bernard and Jensen, or Eaton and Kortum, who are not on this ballot, and how that affects the Helpman-Melitz pairing.
Whether Redding should be added for the quantitative and spatial extensions, or whether that is a separate discovery.
How much weight to give the 2008 trade prize when judging whether selection and reallocation is a distinct advance.
Whether B012 would command broader support if the Committee agreed on a defensible three-person subset of its eight credited names.
How far the robustness concerns about legal-origins regressions in B001 reflect permanent weaknesses rather than normal refinement of a large literature.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My field is behavioural and experimental economics and metascience, with no listed co-authorship or institutional tie to Helpman, Melitz or any other credited candidate on the shortlist.
